question: On 24 November 2025, the Italian Ministry of the Interior ordered the deportation of Mohamed Shahin, an imam who holds a residency permit and has lived in Italy for more than 20 years1. The Ministry of the Interior had classed Mr Shahin as a potential terror threat because of some public statements he had made and used these comments to justify his expulsion.

It seems that political pressure from certain exponents played a part in the decision to deport Imam Shahin, and that this process relied heavily on – and potentially misused – existing counter-terrorism powers. Because he opposes the Egyptian Government, Imam Shahin risks being persecuted and arbitrarily detained if he is deported to his country of origin. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission believe that expelling someone on the basis of their public statements is a course of action that is compatible with the principle of freedom of expression enshrined in Article 11 of the CFR and with the Member State obligations laid down in Article 2 TEU?
How will the Commission ensure that Italy complies with the principle of nonrefoulement laid down in Article 19(2) of the CFR and in the EU laws governing asylum and international protection?
Given that politicians are suspected of having interfered in Mr Shahin’s deportation, will the Commission use the annual rule of law mechanism and other such tools to look into this case?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.2.2026) Member States are responsible for the issuance or withdrawal of residence permits which must respect, where applicable, the relevant Union legislation.

Under Directive 2003/109/EC1, long-term residents may be expelled only if they constitute an actual and sufficiently serious threat to public policy or public security, which is determined in accordance with national law, based on an individual assessment and considering factors such as duration of residence in the territory of the Member State and age.

Member States must also carry out an individual examination under Directive 2008/115/EC2, ensuring that any return or expulsion measure adopted following the withdrawal of a residence permit respects the relevant rules, in particular the principle of non-refoulement.

Therefore, it is for the authorities of Member States to ensure that fundamental rights are respected and protected, subject to the review of judicial authorities, while fulfilling their duty to address serious threats to public policy or public security. The Commission closely monitors the compliance of national legislations and practices with EU law in all Member States and may take action in case of breaches.

It also relies on the Schengen Evaluation Monitoring Mechanism3, which periodically evaluates the implementation of the Schengen acquis in the Member States concerned, including in the area of return.

The annual Rule of Law Report4 monitors developments related to rule of law in Member States, covering four pillars: the justice system, the anti-corruption framework, media pluralism and freedom, and other institutional issues related to checks and balances. However, the Report does not cover the handling of residence permits nor individual cases.
1 Council Directive 2003/109/EC of 25 November 2003 concerning the status of third-country nationals who are

long-term residents; OJ L 16, 23.1.2004. 2 Directive 2008/115/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on common standards and procedures in Member States for returning illegally staying third-country nationals; OK L 348, 24.12.2008.

3 Council Regulation (EU) 2022/922 of 9 June 2022 on the establishment and operation of an evaluation and monitoring mechanism to verify the application of the Schengen acquis, and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1053/2013. 4 https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/upholding-rulelaw/rule-law/annual-rule-law-cycle_en.
